items.headline: July CPI cools modestly, but oil keeps the inflation risk alive
items.summary: U.S. CPI rose 0.1% in July and 3.4% year over year, easing from 3.5% in June and broadly matching expectations. Markets treated the report as sufficiently benign to support equities, but the inflation picture remains vulnerable because Brent is still near USD 89 and Middle East supply disruption is not resolved.
items.whyItMatters: The immediate tail risk of a hot CPI surprise declined, but the policy problem did not disappear. The Fed can remain patient while energy, PPI and core PCE determine whether disinflation is durable or temporary.

items.headline: Hormuz disruption and ship attacks keep crude near the inflation danger zone
items.summary: Brent traded near USD 89 and WTI near USD 84 as attacks on ships and stalled U.S.-Iran diplomacy kept supply-risk premia elevated. Vessel traffic through Hormuz remains far below normal, while U.S. strategic reserves remain constrained relative to historical capacity.
items.whyItMatters: Energy is the most direct channel through which geopolitics can reverse the favorable CPI impulse, lift long yields and pressure margins, consumers and transport-intensive businesses.

items.headline: Japan carry-trade risk becomes a second-order threat to U.S. duration assets
items.summary: Barron's highlights the narrowing yield differential between Japan and the U.S. as a potential threat to yen-funded carry trades. If the Bank of Japan tightens while the Fed stays on hold, leveraged positions in Treasuries and U.S. growth assets could face forced unwinds even without a U.S. rate hike.
items.whyItMatters: The risk is not only the level of U.S. inflation but also global relative rates. A stronger yen and less attractive carry can tighten financial conditions independently of the Fed.

items.headline: CoreWeave validates AI demand but raises the capital-intensity bar
items.summary: CoreWeave reported Q2 revenue of USD 2.58 billion, backlog of USD 104.2 billion and more than USD 25 billion of new commitments, while increasing its 2026 capital-spending plan to USD 35–39 billion. The demand signal is strong, but the scale of capex and ongoing losses keep financing efficiency central to the thesis.
items.whyItMatters: AI infrastructure demand remains real, but the investment case increasingly depends on utilization, cost of capital, contract quality and eventual free cash flow rather than bookings alone.

items.headline: Lumentum shows that optical connectivity remains a high-growth AI bottleneck
items.summary: Lumentum reported quarterly revenue of roughly USD 1.0 billion, more than double a year earlier, with strong earnings and guidance as AI data-center demand drives optical connectivity. The result supports the networking layer of the AI buildout even as valuation and recent price volatility demand discipline.
items.whyItMatters: Compute growth requires bandwidth, switching and optical links. The result broadens the AI beneficiaries beyond GPUs, but high expectations mean entry price matters.

items.headline: Labor-force participation decline adds a structural supply constraint
items.summary: Barron's reports a sharp 2026 decline in U.S. labor-force participation, driven by retirements and immigration-policy effects. Near-term AI displacement remains limited, but reduced labor supply could keep wage and service inflation more persistent than headline employment data imply.
items.whyItMatters: A softer payroll number does not automatically mean slack if labor supply is also shrinking. That complicates rate-cut expectations and reinforces the need to watch participation, wages and productivity together.
